lesson.title: Where 1/sqrt(1 - x^2) Comes From: Differentiating Arcsin
lesson.summary: Applying implicit differentiation to x = sin(y) on the restricted interval where sine is invertible produces the formula d/dx[arcsin(x)] = 1/sqrt(1 - x^2).
lesson.body:
The function arcsin is defined as the inverse of sine restricted to the interval [-pi/2, pi/2] (prerequisite: trigonometric function), the interval on which sine is one-to-one and therefore actually has an inverse, exactly the invertibility condition the Inverse Function Theorem requires. Let y = arcsin(x). By definition of an inverse function, this is the same statement as x = sin(y), with y restricted to [-pi/2, pi/2].

That equation, x = sin(y), is implicit, so differentiate it the same way you differentiated circles and folia earlier in this unit: differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x. The right side needs the chain rule: d/dx[sin(y)] = cos(y) (dy/dx). The left side is d/dx[x] = 1. So cos(y) (dy/dx) = 1, which gives dy/dx = 1/cos(y).

That answer is in terms of y, but arcsin(x) should have a derivative in terms of x. Use the Pythagorean identity sin^2(y) + cos^2(y) = 1, so cos(y) = plus or minus sqrt(1 - sin^2(y)) = plus or minus sqrt(1 - x^2), since sin(y) = x. Because y is restricted to [-pi/2, pi/2], cosine is never negative there, so the correct sign is the positive root: cos(y) = sqrt(1 - x^2). Substituting back:

d/dx[arcsin(x)] = 1/sqrt(1 - x^2), for -1 < x < 1

Test it at x = 1/2. Directly from the formula: 1/sqrt(1 - (1/2)^2) = 1/sqrt(3/4) = 1/(sqrt(3)/2) = 2/sqrt(3) = 2 sqrt(3)/3, which is about 1.1547. As a cross check using the definition, arcsin(1/2) = pi/6, since sin(pi/6) = 1/2, and cos(pi/6) = sqrt(3)/2, so dy/dx = 1/cos(y) = 1/(sqrt(3)/2) = 2/sqrt(3), the same value. At the endpoints x = 1 and x = -1, the formula's denominator hits 0, matching cos(y) = 0 at y = pi/2 and y = -pi/2, the points where sine's tangent line is horizontal and arcsin's tangent line is correspondingly vertical, the same exception the Inverse Function Theorem predicts. When x is replaced by some other differentiable function u(x), the ordinary chain rule extends this to d/dx[arcsin(u)] = u'/sqrt(1 - u^2).
